messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst, had always been a man of routine and precision. His life was marked by stability until the day his wife, Mary, passed away suddenly from a heart attack. The memory of that fateful evening remained seared in his mind—a vivid snapshot of the ambulance sirens wailing into the night, the paramedics rushing in and out of their home, and the finality of the hospital's sterile walls as they confirmed her passing. In the months following Mary’s death, John found himself increasingly triggered by loss themes. Simple conversations at work about retirement plans or family events would send his mind spiraling back to that night. The sight of a funeral procession on the way to his office or the mention of a colleague's recent bereavement would suddenly bring the memory flooding back. These intrusive thoughts were not just memories; they were visceral, bringing with them a wave of intense negative emotions—fear, horror, and an overwhelming sense of guilt for not being able to save her. Each trigger seemed to amplify his physical reactivity, causing his heart to race and his hands to tremble as if he were reliving the trauma. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, John began to numb himself emotionally. He threw himself into work, staying late at the office and avoiding any social gatherings that might remind him of Mary. When a coworker suggested they visit a local cemetery on a Sunday afternoon to pay respects to a mutual friend’s loved one, John declined, citing an urgent project deadline. The thought of being in a place associated with loss was too much to bear. He also found himself suppressing thoughts of the trauma, often catching himself mid-thought and quickly redirecting his mind to work-related tasks. John’s emotional numbing and avoidance behaviors only served to heighten his sensitivity to triggers. By avoiding grief reminders, he inadvertently created an environment where even the smallest cues could set off a chain reaction. A casual mention of a lost pet in a news article or a passing comment about someone moving away would send him into a spiral of negative emotions. The more he tried to suppress these thoughts, the stronger they became, leading to increased irritability and angry outbursts at home and work. One particularly difficult day, John’s manager approached him with concerns about his recent performance. The stress of constantly managing triggers and suppressing thoughts had taken its toll, affecting his concentration and decision-making skills. This feedback was a turning point for John. Realizing that his maladaptive strategies were not only failing to alleviate his suffering but also impacting his professional life, he finally decided to seek help. John’s current state is one of deep ambivalence. On one hand, he is afraid that therapy will force him to confront the very memories and emotions he has been trying so hard to avoid. On the other hand, he is desperate for a way to break the cycle of triggers, negative emotions, and maladaptive coping mechanisms that have dominated his life since Mary’s passing. He hopes that with professional support, he can find a path forward—one where the memory of his beloved wife does not continue to overshadow every aspect of his daily existence.
